title: Two monks and a river
hook: Tanzan carries a woman across a stream, and hours later Ekido is still carrying her in his head (Zen story, Japan)
carry: I set her down at the river

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shoshin, beginner's mind: Nan-in poured tea until it spilled. Your line was empty the cup.

Two in the morning. Someone lies awake replaying a remark from lunch. Or from last week. Or from years ago. The person who said it has long forgotten it, and is fast asleep. And the remark is still being turned over, carried around the dark room. Now, two monks walking home in the rain, Tanzan and Ekido. The water is high and the road is a mess, and at the crossing stands a young woman in a silk kimono who can't get across. Tanzan does something his companion will not stop thinking about for hours.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, REPLAYING.` → `TANZAN AND EKIDO.` → `A WOMAN WHO CAN'T CROSS.`

segments.voice: Tanzan doesn't hesitate. Come on, he says. He picks her up, carries her across the water, sets her down on the other side, and walks on. Ekido says nothing, all afternoon, all the way to the temple. But he's boiling. These monks had vowed to keep their distance from women, and his companion just picked one up in the road. That night he can't hold it in. We monks aren't supposed to go near women, he says. Especially not young and lovely ones. Why did you do that? And Tanzan answers: I set her down at the river. Are you still carrying her? A word on the details: in the twentieth-century English telling, the crossing is a flooded, muddy road; later retellings made it a river, and the river stuck. Tanzan is remembered as a real Zen teacher with a habit of breaking conventions. Now look who's really carrying the woman. Tanzan held her for a minute, to help, and let her go. Ekido never touched her, and he carried her for hours in his head, heavier with every step. The weight wasn't in the act. It was in the holding on. The old insult. The awkward moment. The thing you should have said. The thing that was done, and finished, long ago. Zen teachers have a word for letting go: hōge, casting down.
screen: `HE CARRIES HER ACROSS.` · `EKIDO BOILS ALL AFTERNOON.` · `ARE YOU STILL CARRYING HER?` · `THE WEIGHT IS IN THE HOLDING ON.` · then, large: `I SET HER DOWN AT THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Find something that happened, and is over, but that you're still holding, a remark, a mistake, an argument that ended days ago, and feel where you carry it: shoulders, jaw, stomach. Then picture a river, walk to the far bank, and set it down on the ground there. You don't have to forget it; just stop carrying it for now.
Hōge, the Zen word for letting go, casting down. Tanzan sets the woman down at the river; Ekido carries her in his head all day.
Your line: I set her down at the river. Ekido never even touched her. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Zen teachers tell the story of Tanzan and Ekido when talking about letting go, and in meditation practice people notice a thought they keep returning to and set it down, again and again.

notes: The best-known English version (Zen Flesh, Zen Bones, 'Muddy Road') is not public domain and has a muddy road, not a river; the script says so and paraphrases.
Tanzan (Hara Tanzan, 1819–1892) described as a real, unconventional teacher of 19th-century Japan; confirm. Ekido's historicity not claimed.
Japanese 放下 (hōge; also 放下著 hōgejaku) as the Zen word for letting go: confirm spelling and reading.
Carry has capital I, allowed by the guide ('I').
